title: 1 Samuel 26:13–25
context: From a safe distance across the valley, David calls out to Abner for failing to guard the king and shows Saul’s spear and water jar as proof that he could have killed him. Saul recognizes his voice, and David pleads his innocence, asking why the king pursues him and asking that, if the LORD has stirred Saul up against him, an offering be accepted, but if men have done it, they be cursed for driving him from the LORD’s inheritance. Saul confesses that he has sinned and played the fool, blesses David, and the two part ways for the last time recorded in the book. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read this passage as shared ground about vindication left to God and integrity in the face of injustice. David’s conditional words in verse 19 are commonly read as an honest recognition that God may use even hostile circumstances, without settling how God and human agents are related.

verses.text: Then David went over to the other side, and stood on the top of the mountain far away, a great space being between them;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David crossing to the far side and standing on a mountaintop at a safe distance. Wisdom keeps him out of reach.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the distance as prudent and as setting the stage for a public confrontation. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a narrative transition.

verses.text: and David cried to the people, and to Abner the son of Ner, saying, “Don’t you answer, Abner?” Then Abner answered, “Who are you who calls to the king?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David calling out to the people and to Abner, who asks who is calling to the king. David seeks a hearing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the exchange as drawing attention to Abner’s failure as Saul’s protector. Both traditions commonly read the verse as preparing for David’s rebuke.

verses.text: David said to Abner, “Aren’t you a man? Who is like you in Israel? Why then have you not kept watch over your lord the king? For one of the people came in to destroy your lord the king.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David challenging Abner for failing to guard the king, noting that someone came to destroy him. David exposes the weakness of Saul’s defenses.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the rebuke as making clear that only God’s restraint, and David’s, preserved Saul. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse with a note of irony.

verses.text: This thing isn’t good that you have done. As the LORD lives, you are worthy to die, because you have not kept watch over your lord, the LORD’s anointed. Now see where the king’s spear is, and the jar of water that was at his head.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David declaring that Abner is worthy of death for not protecting the LORD’s anointed. He shows the spear and jar as evidence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David’s words as underscoring his own respect for the anointed king. Both traditions commonly read the verse as vindicating David’s integrity before witnesses.

verses.text: Saul recognized David’s voice, and said, “Is this your voice, my son David?” David said, “It is my voice, my lord, O king.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Saul recognizing David’s voice and calling him my son, echoing the earlier scene at En Gedi (1 Samuel 24:16). Relationship is briefly restored.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the recognition as setting up another moment of confession from Saul. Readers in both traditions commonly see a mixture of affection and instability in Saul’s words.

verses.text: He said, “Why does my lord pursue his servant? For what have I done? What evil is in my hand?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David asking why Saul pursues him and what evil is in his hand. He appeals to his innocence before the king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David’s questions as a plea for justice grounded in a clear conscience. Both traditions commonly read the verse as an honest protest against unjust persecution.

verses.text: Now therefore, please let my lord the king hear the words of his servant. If it is so that the LORD has stirred you up against me, let him accept an offering. But if it is the children of men, they are cursed before the LORD; for they have driven me out today that I shouldn’t cling to the LORD’s inheritance, saying, ‘Go, serve other gods!’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David considering whether the LORD has stirred Saul against him, in which case an offering might be accepted, or whether men are responsible and stand cursed. He recognizes both possibilities without claiming to know which is true.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in David’s words a recognition that God can use even hostile circumstances for his purposes (compare 1 Samuel 16:14; 2 Samuel 24:1). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as honest reflection rather than a settled statement about how God and human agents relate.

verses.text: Now therefore, don’t let my blood fall to the earth away from the presence of the LORD; for the king of Israel has come out to seek a flea, as when one hunts a partridge in the mountains.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David asking that his blood not fall away from the LORD’s presence, comparing himself to a flea or a partridge. He stresses how small a threat he is.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David’s vivid comparisons as appealing to Saul’s sense of proportion. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a humble plea for mercy.

verses.text: Then Saul said, “I have sinned. Return, my son David; for I will no more do you harm, because my life was precious in your eyes today. Behold, I have played the fool, and have erred exceedingly.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Saul confessing that he has sinned and played the fool, promising no more harm. His words are striking, though his record suggests they may not last.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Saul’s confession as genuine in the moment yet not leading to lasting change (compare 1 Samuel 15:24; 2 Corinthians 7:10). Readers in both traditions commonly read it as a sobering picture of regret without full repentance.

verses.text: David answered, “Behold the spear, O king! Let one of the young men come over and get it.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David inviting a young man to come and retrieve the spear. He returns what belongs to the king and keeps nothing for himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the return of the spear as a final demonstration of David’s integrity. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing restraint and respect.

verses.text: The LORD will give to every man his righteousness and his faithfulness; because the LORD delivered you into my hand today, and I wouldn’t stretch out my hand against the LORD’s anointed.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David trusting that the LORD will reward righteousness and faithfulness, since he refused to harm the anointed. Integrity is entrusted to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David’s confidence that God rewards faithfulness (compare Psalm 18:20). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as affirming that God sees and honors righteous restraint.

verses.text: Behold, as your life was respected today in my eyes, so let my life be respected in the LORD’s eyes, and let him deliver me out of all oppression.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David asking that as he valued Saul’s life, the LORD would value his. He commits his safety to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David entrusting himself to God’s deliverance rather than Saul’s promises. Both traditions commonly see this as a model of committing oneself to the one who judges righteously (compare 1 Peter 2:23).

verses.text: Then Saul said to David, “You are blessed, my son David. You will both do mightily, and will surely prevail.” So David went his way, and Saul returned to his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Saul blessing David and predicting his success before they part. The two go separate ways, and this is the last meeting between them recorded in the book.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Saul’s blessing as unwittingly affirming God’s purpose for David. Readers in both traditions commonly read the parting as a quiet close to David’s long season of restraint toward Saul.
